GPU memory: one 2,520-patch image needs about 610 MB of attention buffer per vision layer on ONNX Runtime CUDA; a vision batch of two failed with about 5.5 GB free in the spike. EmbeddingGemma2MultimodalOptions.MaxVisionBatchSize defaults to 1; the three graphs take about 2.9 GB of GPU memory when text-only inputs are also embedded.
Native runtime: Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime.Gpu.Linux 1.30.0 needs the CUDA 13 runtime and cuDNN 9 on the loader path; the package does not ship them.

Evaluator run 2026-10-11 (docs/evidence/embeddinggemma2-dotnet/, CPU): G1 passed; G2 failed only on export.token_embeddings (Python ORT vs PyTorch): the tolerance file's |d| <= 1e-4 * max(1, |ref|) judged per value gives 1.7e-2, while the per-case max |d| / max(1, max |ref|) the bound was set from is 6.2e-6. Which reading binds is a maintainer decision; every .NET check passed.

The hosted graph is public since 2026-10-14. The 0.1.0-preview.6 release drill downloaded it with no token into an empty cache, verified it and ran the sample offline (Linux x64, one machine); other platforms are untested.

Fixtures reach 1,750 tokens and batch-independence checks 2,049; 2,050 to 8,192 tokens has no reference evidence. One 8,192-token row took 80 s on the 12-thread workstation CPU (process peak working set 5.9 GB during the test run); temporary memory grows with the square of the length in the full-attention layers.

The fixtures cover the none, query and document prompts only; the other 18 names map to prompt texts without fixture rows. Matryoshka sizes are checked against the reference sliced and renormalized (the fixtures hold no truncated rows; the spike probe showed sentence-transformers truncate_dim equals that within 6e-8).

Synthetic fixture videos only (no camera footage); default settings only; no variable frame rate, interlaced or HDR video. One CPU architecture (AVX2) produced the reference and the decoder comparison: swscale's SIMD paths on other CPUs (ARM in particular) may differ by a level, for upstream as well.

One decoder profile per FFmpeg adapter: decoder_ffmpeg (FFmpeg 8, libavcodec.so.62) is protected; decoder_ffmpeg9 (FFmpeg 9, libavcodec.so.63) is proposed and waits for the maintainer to commit it, so G1 does not yet cover the FFmpeg 9 adapter. Its exactness evidence used the machine's FFmpeg 9.0.1 distribution build (GPL, loaded with AllowNonLgplBuild); no LGPL FFmpeg 9 build was tested.
CPU video embedding is slow: the vision tower dominates (about 2.7 s per 1,260-patch frame on an i7-5820K), so a 32-frame video takes about 100 s; prefer CUDA for video.

Results are ordered by confidence; most entity scores saturate to exactly 1.0 in fp32, so near-ties make the order sensitive to backend noise (ORT CUDA with TF32 reorders one 1,329-token case with the same entity set).

Upstream span offsets index the normalized text: a span that includes the appended '.' ends one past the original text (seen at threshold 0.0). The C# package maps such spans onto the input (behavior.defaults).

The pinned tokenizer.json emits a lone "▁" token before special-token literals and for trailing whitespace, where SentencePiece and transformers 5.18 emit none. The owned profile follows tokenizer.json; the difference is recorded, not fixed.
tokenizer.json leaves decomposed Hangul jamo uncomposed, while SentencePiece composes them.

Native runtime: Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime.Gpu 1.30.0 needs CUDA 13 runtime libraries and cuDNN 9 on the loader path; the package does not ship them. The schema has no field for native runtime, driver or GPU requirements, so they are recorded here and in docs/m0/e5-gpu.md.
With use_tf32 0, ORT CUDA matches the PyTorch fp32 CPU hidden states to 2.1e-6 and the protected embeddings to 1.9e-7 on the M0 corpus; C# and Python ORT CUDA hidden states are bit-identical.
The ONNX Runtime GenAI C# API is labeled preview upstream; Starlings.Generation.OnnxGenAI isolates it. The runtime version must equal the builder version that wrote the graph (0.17.1).
